title: Embedding flow moderator: proactive burst control, tenant headroom and micro-batching policy
creator: Avery Chen
description:
Background:
We continue to see tenant-driven microbursts and hotkey traffic patterns that cause transient p99 regressions and uneven slot utilization for the embeddings service. Existing autoscalers react too slowly at the millisecond-to-second scale and our queueing logic can overcommit memory when many small requests arrive simultaneously. This ticket defines a 'flow moderator' subsystem to sit in the embedding ingress path and provide proactive burst control, tenant headroom reservation, and adaptive micro-batching heuristics to stabilize latency and make autoscaling more predictable.

Goals / Success metrics:
- Reduce embedding p99 latency variance by 35% for tenants with bursty traffic within 30 days of rollout.
- Decrease extraneous scale-ups (nodes spun due to short bursts) by 40% for 90% of tenants.
- Keep steady-state cost within 5% of current baseline while improving tail latency.
- No increase in error rate or client-facing 429s beyond planned soft-throttle behavior.

Design overview:
1) Flow moderator (FM) core: lightweight admission controller deployed per-ingress tier that maintains per-tenant moving-window stats (request rate, mean token length, recent latencies) and computes: headroom reservation, short-term burst budget, and batching hints.
2) Proactive burst control: FM grants a transient 'burst token' allowance to tenants when sudden rate increases are detected; tokens are consumed to allow short-lived bursts without triggering immediate autoscaler growth. When budget is exhausted FM starts soft-throttling with graceful 429-with-retry-after responses and a queue hint for SDKs.
3) Tenant headroom reservation: the FM will reserve fractional concurrency budget for tenants with historically bursty profiles so ephemeral spikes absorb into reserved headroom rather than alerting the cluster autoscaler. Reservations are kept small (configurable percent of pool) and subject to decay if unused.
4) Micro-batching policy: FM emits batching suggestions to the router that group requests arriving within tight time windows when latency budget allows. Policy uses token lengths and client latency SLO to decide batching size; uses a fast-path for single-request low-latency workloads to avoid added jitter.
5) Autoscaler integration: expose short-lived synthetic signals (burst-adjusted RPS and headroom consumption) to the autoscaler to avoid overreacting to burst traffic. Autoscaler will require a new smoothing policy to respect synthetic signals for a short cooldown.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Memory vs accuracy: FM keeps only sliding-window aggregates (not per-request traces) to limit memory overhead. This trades off fidelity for operational safety.
- Soft-throttling vs strict dropping: prefer soft 429 + retry hints to maintain graceful client behavior and give SDKs an opportunity to backoff.
- Batching-induced latency vs throughput: batching only when predicted latency impact < configured SLO; default conservative thresholds to prioritize p99 performance.

Implementation plan (phases):
A. Prototype (week 1-2): implement FM core as a Go service adjacent to the existing ingress, with in-memory sliding windows and a simple burst token algorithm. Add feature flags to enable per-tenant headroom.
B. Canary (week 3): rollout to low-traffic region and 5 internal tenants. Collect telemetry (p99, scale events, throttles).
C. Gradual rollout (week 4-6): expand to 25% of tenants with monitoring dashboards and automated rollback if p99 regressions exceed 10%.
D. Full rollout and autoscaler tweak (week 7-8): enable autoscaler smoothing policy cluster-wide, tune defaults.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for token bucket and headroom decay logic.
- Integration tests simulating burst patterns (sawtooth, power-law, hotkey single-tenant).
- Load tests using k6 + protobuf traffic generator to measure scale-up events and p99.
- Client SDK test to ensure 429+retry-after behavior is handled gracefully.

Monitoring / Observability:
- New Grafana panels: per-tenant headroom usage, burst token burn rate, FM soft-throttle rate, synthetic autoscaler signals.
- Alerts: sustained headroom depletion for >1m, >5% increase in scale events compared to baseline, unexpected increase in 5xx or 429s.

Rollout kill-switches and safety:
- Feature flag to disable FM per-cluster and per-tenant.
- Auto rollback: if canary's p99 increases by >10% for 5 consecutive minutes, automatically disable FM for canary group.

Documentation and SDK changes:
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Embedding+Flow+Moderator+Design
- SDK change: surface Retry-After advisory in embeddings SDKs and add opt-in batching hints API. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/embeddings-sdk/pull/1298

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default headroom percent per pool (proposal: 5%)
- Maximum burst token lifetime (proposal: 7s)
- Whether to persist per-tenant profiles to Redis for cross-process continuity or keep ephemeral in-memory state (prefers in-memory initially).

Next steps:
- Finish prototype and demo to PM and infra on 2026-02-20.
- Schedule canary window and coordinate with SRE for autoscaler policy changes.
